candidate_sources.title: Birch - Marssonina Leaf Spot - University of Maine Cooperative Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Small dark spots develop on leaves; spots enlarge and coalesce as masses of necrotic tissue, leading to premature defoliation. Pathogen is Marssonina spp. Overwinters in infected leaf debris and shoots; spring spores spread by wind and rain.

candidate_sources.title: Marssonina betulae / Leaf spot pathogen
candidate_sources.snippet: Marssonina betulae causes leaf spot of birch. Initial symptoms are small black spots that enlarge and join together as a mass of necrotic tissue, with complete defoliation occurring during summer; sometimes bark necrosis and twig canker.

candidate_sources.title: Birch Leaf Spot. Marssonina Betulae. (Factsheet PDF)
candidate_sources.snippet: Birch Leaf Spot is a foliar disease caused by Marssonina betulae affecting Birch, Aspen and Cottonwood. Mainly affects European birch (Betula pendula) and cultivars. Dissemination via windborne spores overwintering in dormant buds and twigs. Management: rake fallen leaves, prune cankered stems, fungicide at budbreak.

candidate_sources.title: 1476 – Marssonina leaf spot – PlantTalk Colorado
candidate_sources.snippet: Small dark-brown spots, often with yellow margins, develop on young leaves in spring; spots may coalesce into larger lesions and cause premature leaf drop. The fungus overwinters in infected leaf debris on the ground.

candidate_sources.title: Microsphaera penicillata - Bugwoodwiki
candidate_sources.snippet: Microsphaera penicillata (now Erysiphe penicillata) and Phyllactinia guttata produce white mycelial growth on leaves, buds, flowers, and new stems. Symptoms include white powdery growth on either leaf surface, with sparse mycelial growth and dark, spherical chasmothecia obvious especially on the underside of leaves late in the growing season, infecting hosts including Betula (birch) and Alnus (alder).

candidate_sources.title: Powdery Mildew : Landscape : Center for Agriculture, Food, and the Environment (CAFE) at UMass Amherst
candidate_sources.snippet: Birch (Betula) is a common host in the managed landscape for powdery mildew infections. White to gray powdery patches appear on affected tissues, and infected leaves may show yellowish or purple spots. Infections can reduce growth, cause foliar scorch, premature leaf drop, and stem dieback, though most often the disease is cosmetic.

candidate_sources.title: powdery mildew (Phyllactinia guttata (Wallr.) Lév.)
candidate_sources.snippet: Powdery mildew on birch is caused by Phyllactinia guttata, a fungus in the Erysiphaceae that produces white to gray powdery patches on leaves and stems of a broad range of hosts including Betula. Dark spherical fruiting bodies (chasmothecia) form on the underside of leaves late in the season.
